overview: The exact atlas id “nepal-1492” lasts only from 1492 to 1500. Its eight-position polygon is a coarse western Himalayan display shape, not modern Nepal and not one Malla kingdom. Tested Nuwakot, Pokhara, Jumla, Doti, and Lumbini lie inside; Kathmandu, Patan, Bhaktapur, Kirtipur, Banepa, Lo Manthang, and the eastern and southern lowlands do not. The exclusion matters because much surviving late-fifteenth-century evidence describes the Kathmandu Valley. There, Yaksha Malla's former realm had already divided into competing courts at Bhaktapur, Kathmandu, and Patan. Communities inside the polygon belonged to distinct local political landscapes; the drawn shape does not make them one government or one everyday culture. Routes, manuscripts, religious traditions, and skilled craft connected particular places without erasing those differences. The eight annual teaching windows reflect the atlas interval, not eight securely documented yearly revolutions. Surviving evidence is uneven: courts and religious institutions speak louder than children, women, farmers, porters, or remote households. At 1500 the id vanishes; its tested points switch to broad Tibet and Delhi Sultanate labels. That is an atlas seam, not a conquest, national birth, or social collapse.

periods.title: 1492 to 1493: a short atlas window opens
periods.summary: The map introduces one western Himalayan shape after Valley-wide Malla rule had already ended. Academic accounts distinguish rival Valley courts and urban cultures, so this first annual bucket teaches parallel authorities rather than one successor state. No separate event is securely assigned to every place in this polygon.

periods.title: 1493 to 1494: Raya Malla grants land
periods.summary: A copper-plate inscription dated Nepal Samvat 614, corresponding to 1493/94, records Raya Malla granting land for Shiva worship at Yaksheshvara in Bhaktapur. It names the royal family and an announcement before subjects. This is unusually precise court evidence, but Bhaktapur lies outside the atlas polygon.

periods.title: 1494 to 1495: cities and buildings outlast one court
periods.summary: Architectural research places Kathmandu, Patan, and Bhaktapur in a landscape of emerging city-states and warns that the familiar story of Yaksha Malla simply dividing one kingdom among sons is too tidy. Surviving buildings also have layered repairs and disputed dates, so one quiet year should not invite invention.

periods.title: 1495 to 1496: a manuscript names Raya Malla
periods.summary: A Gita Govinda manuscript dated Nepal Samvat 616, corresponding to 1495/96, says it was copied in the reign of Raya Malla. Its short Sanskrit colophon securely names a ruler and date. It does not reveal how many people could read, what language families spoke, or who made the writing material.

periods.title: 1496 to 1497: manuscripts move through connected worlds
periods.summary: Manuscript colophons show donors, monasteries, and books participating in networks between the Kathmandu Valley, northern India, and trans-Himalayan regions. This annual bucket marks continuing exchange rather than a newly discovered 1497 event. A traveling book proves circulation; it does not prove that every household traveled or read.

periods.title: 1497 to 1498: western places remain a source problem
periods.summary: The polygon includes tested Jumla and Doti while excluding every tested Kathmandu Valley city. That geometry warns against filling a western annual bucket with Valley court history. The atlas supplies no distinct 1497 event, frontier survey, or shared government for the included communities, so the card preserves the uncertainty.

periods.title: 1498 to 1499: pilgrimage continues at Lumbini
periods.summary: Lumbini lies inside the tested polygon. Archaeology documents Buddhist monasteries through the fifth century and stupas continuing through the fifteenth, so pilgrimage memory and sacred building endured near this interval. The evidence does not identify a 1498 patron or make the site proof that every point inside shared one ruler.

periods.title: 1499 to 1500: the feature ends, communities continue
periods.summary: At the endpoint the exact id disappears. Nuwakot, Pokhara, and Jumla become “tibet,” while Doti and Lumbini become “delhi-sultanate” in the atlas. Kathmandu Valley probes remain outside the target. These are software assignments, not evidence that two empires conquered all five places on New Year's Day 1500.

sections.title: Read the atlas before reading the history

items.text: The live index has one exact “nepal-1492” record named “Nepal,” circa 1492 to 1500. Coverage records one border file, while the exact card and researched override are absent. Its imported summary describes the modern multilingual country, so this packet replaces that collision instead of quietly carrying it into the Middle Ages.

The 1492 target is one Polygon with one ring and eight decoded positions. Its bounding box runs from 80.10260102601029, 27.27706261766734 to 85.86265862658627, 30.191319255656083. The decoded geometry SHA-256 is b2cd2aec60caa3cae98828373a1f0adca6172108a10a7cef67bf17f1f67fd91a. Those are dataset facts, not surveyed medieval boundaries.

Tested Nuwakot, Pokhara, Jumla, Doti, and Lumbini are inside. Kathmandu, Patan, Bhaktapur, Kirtipur, Banepa, Lo Manthang, Nepalgunj, Simraungadh, Janakpur, Biratnagar, Khasa, Shigatse, and Varanasi are outside. The map therefore excludes the Kathmandu Valley communities that dominate the late Malla written record.

The target shares encoded arcs only with atlas features called “tibet” and “delhi-sultanate.” In both 1400 and 1492 the Kathmandu Valley probes fall under the Tibet color, while southern and eastern owners vary. These labels describe a generalized map, not uniform tribute, occupation, ethnicity, language, or belief.

Separate ids named “nepal,” “nepal-1492,” and “nepal-1650” appear in 1200, 1492, and 1650 snapshots, with absences at their endpoints. The first two reuse a coarse footprint; the third changes its northern edge. Intermittent colors do not prove one continuous state waiting politely between map files.

Yaksha Malla's death preceded competing centers of rule, but surviving manuscripts and later chronicles do not support a perfectly clean three-son partition. Raya Malla is associated with Bhaktapur and Ratna Malla with Kathmandu; Patan and Banepa had their own powerful actors. “The three kingdoms” is useful shorthand, not a complete constitutional diagram.

The atlas index begins this exact feature in 1492, but neither the index nor the border file records a foundation ceremony, ruler, or constitutional change in that year. The start date organizes display coverage. It cannot fill later annual gaps, and it should not be mistaken for the birth of a state.

Raya Malla's 1493/94 grant was made with royal relatives present and announced before subjects, revealing a Bhaktapur court, religious patronage, and a public political act. It does not demonstrate command over Nuwakot, Jumla, Doti, Lumbini, or other places inside the map shape, none of which the document makes his uniform territory.

Jumla and Doti test inside the polygon, while Kathmandu, Patan, and Bhaktapur test outside. That result alone defeats a Valley-centered reading of the whole feature. The label “Nepal” is atlas shorthand here; it does not make one named Malla ruler, law, tax system, or court govern every included place.

Oxford's history presents the late Malla Valley as rival kingdoms with their own political structures and urban cultures. That frame matters here: neighboring courts could share temples, monasteries, artists, and languages without forming one state. Political vocabulary stays local because the atlas shape and modern Nepal's government did not define their authority.

sections.title: Towns, routes, trade, and regional variety

items.text: Kathmandu, Patan, and Bhaktapur were important urban centers, but every one lies outside this exact polygon. Academic history treats them as rival Malla courts with distinct political structures. Their evidence supplies neighboring context, not permission to repaint the target as a Kathmandu-centered state or assume that every city followed identical rules.

The Kathmandu Valley's fertile soil and position across routes toward Tibet supported unusual urban specialization. Inscriptions and Newari place-names reveal long literacy and settlement histories. This describes the excluded Valley, while the hills and western basins inside the target had different densities, work patterns, and access to long-distance exchange.

Tucci describes Nepal as a cultural intermediary between India and Tibet, visible in manuscripts, inscriptions, religion, and art. “Intermediary” means people, objects, and ideas crossed particular routes; it does not mean all transit passed through one court. Porters, merchants, monks, and craftspeople remain less named than elite patrons in the evidence.

Lumbini's archaeological area preserves a long pilgrimage history, with monastic remains and stupas spanning many centuries. Because the tested point sits inside the target, it adds a lowland sacred landscape to the card. It does not prove Malla administration, shared taxation, or the everyday religion of western hill households.

The polygon stretches from far-western Doti through Jumla and Pokhara toward Nuwakot, while excluding Lo Manthang, Nepalgunj, and the Kathmandu Valley cities. Its span suggests very different terrain and access, but geometry is not a route map. It cannot supply a caravan timetable, customs post, travel time, or common market.

sections.title: Religion, literature, art, craft, and discovery

items.text: The Met's survey of Nepalese painting follows Buddhist and Hindu commissions across manuscript illustrations, painted book covers, and cloth paintings. That evidence makes religious patronage and workshop skill visible in the Kathmandu Valley. It does not establish one ritual mix, temple plan, or devotional routine for every community inside the western polygon.

Newar artists made manuscript illustrations, painted book covers, and cloth paintings for Buddhist and Hindu patrons. The Met identifies a distinctive fifteenth-century development in rich decoration and precise brushwork. That achievement belongs to skilled workshops and patrons in the Kathmandu Valley, outside the exact polygon, and cannot describe every western craft tradition.

A sixteenth-century Malla-period Bhairava in copper alloy demonstrates the virtuosity for which Newari metalworkers became known across the Himalayas. The object postdates 1492 to 1500, so it serves as later craft context only. A shiny survivor is excellent evidence for technique, but a terrible population census.

Architectural study describes Valley buildings made with earth in brick and tile together with timber, and it warns that famous structures have layered repairs and disputed dates. Materials can illuminate craft continuity. Assigning a photographed, rebuilt, or later palace unchanged to a 1490s household would still be architectural time travel.

Modern discovery has shaped what can be told. Tucci's field study brought attention to Malla inscriptions and monuments, while manuscript cataloging recovered dated colophons that anchor rulers. Discovery here means scholars finding and interpreting surviving evidence, not medieval people suddenly inventing their own temples, books, or artistic skill.

sections.title: Farming, environment, food, and connected work

items.text: Rolled palm-leaf deeds preserve land transactions, loans, property transfers, and other agreements across the Malla centuries. They reveal an economy in which households and institutions managed valuable rights in writing. Their long date range does not provide a precise 1492 crop yield, rent, or family field size across the polygon.

The Valley's exceptional fertility helped support dense towns and a division of labor among farmers, merchants, and craftspeople. That relationship explains neighboring Malla urbanism. The polygon itself stretches across western hills and the Terai, so Valley soil and market density cannot be copied across the shape like one giant agricultural recipe.

The decoded shape spans western hills and a narrow lowland edge, but its eight points contain no fields, terraces, herd counts, or harvest records. The map supports geographic caution, not an environmental reconstruction. Crops, livestock, household labor, and seasonal shortages in this short interval remain unevenly documented.

Neither the exact index nor the border file supplies a shared 1490s menu, and the reviewed period evidence does not repair that silence across the whole polygon. Modern dishes cannot simply be carried backward. History may be hungry for detail, but it still needs permission before raiding a medieval lunch basket.

Network studies make circulation visible through manuscript colophons, production places, patrons, and religious institutions. They reveal connected work without supplying a payroll. Porters, pack-animal handlers, road maintainers, and household laborers remain harder to identify, so the card does not invent wages, work hours, or equal access across the included principalities.

sections.title: Families, women, associations, and social life

items.text: The 1493/94 Bhaktapur grant says Raya Malla acted with the royal family present. That is direct evidence for a courtly kin group participating in a public religious gift. It is not a model household: the document does not tell us how farmers divided childcare, how spouses negotiated property, or what most homes looked like.

Malla-period rolled palm-leaf deeds record land transactions, loans, property transfers, and other agreements. Those documents show that households and institutions managed valuable rights in writing. The collection spans the thirteenth to eighteenth centuries, so it proves a documentary tradition, not that every surviving deed or legal formula belonged to 1492.

Guthi associations could finance worship, festivals, funerals, roads, shelters, and charitable purposes through land and member obligations. An ethnohistorical synthesis also warns that their structure changed after the Malla era. The card therefore treats guthi as a durable institutional family of practices, not a frozen rulebook for every 1490s neighborhood.

Later descriptions say guthi membership could follow family and marriage ties, with rank and duties organized by seniority. Because these observations are not a 1490s household survey, they cannot establish one marriage pattern, women's experience, or children's role across the period. They instead show which questions surviving land and ritual institutions can help historians ask.

Preserved catalogs and manuscripts name texts, rulers, donors, scribes, and learned specialists more readily than ordinary households. Women, children, servants, cultivators, porters, and low-status workers appear less often. Documentary silence measures preservation and power as much as population; an unnamed life is not an absent life.

sections.title: Children, learning, manuscripts, and written language

items.text: Modern manuscript scholarship examines medieval Nepalese book production, readers, editors, and scribal intervention. Those fields make advanced learned work visible without turning every religious institution into a modern school. The reviewed evidence does not establish age grades, classrooms, universal enrollment, or equal access for children across the polygon.

The Durbar Library catalog lists texts on religion, medicine, astronomy, drama, poetry, rhetoric, and politics. Such range suggests advanced specialist learning and copying. It does not show a curriculum for every child, a literacy rate, or equal access by gender and status; preserved libraries heavily favor learned and elite production.

Modern manuscript scholarship studies collections, codicology, readers, editors, scribal intervention, and the production of medieval Nepalese works. A surviving book was a material object and an edited text, not a transparent transcript. Palm leaf offered no convenient undo button, so corrections and layout choices became evidence for how people worked.

Written-language sample, shown in modern Devanagari normalization: “राज्ये श्री जय रायमल्ल नृपतेः.” Transliteration: “rājye Śrī Jaya Rāyamalla nṛpateḥ.” Meaning: “in the reign of King Śrī Jaya Rāyamalla.” It comes from a Gita Govinda colophon dated Nepal Samvat 616, 1495/96, in the Bhaktapur ruler's manuscript context.

The printed source gives the colophon in Roman transcription; the Devanagari above is a modern normalization, not a facsimile of the manuscript's original letterforms. It is learned Sanskrit, not a sample of everyone's speech. Palaeographic research also warns that scripts, hands, and dating must be compared across dated witnesses.

sections.title: Homes, clothing, crafts, and daily routines

items.text: Architectural research describes Newar buildings from farmhouse to palace as using earth in brick and tile together with timber. Dense Valley towns packed houses along narrow streets. This is useful neighboring context, while the western polygon held different settlements. The evidence does not supply one universal floor plan, room count, or sleeping arrangement.

Rolled palm-leaf documents preserve property and credit agreements rather than room-by-room household descriptions. They show that durable records mattered to families and institutions, but they do not reveal a universal floor plan, sleeping arrangement, storage system, or guest room. Legal survival is not a complete tour of a home.

Manuscript scholarship reconstructs preparation, copying, correction, reading, and preservation as skilled material work. That supports bookmaking craft, not a complete clothing history. Exact 1490s garment cuts, children's dress, loom ownership, work hours, and the division of textile labor remain too thinly documented for confident reconstruction.

Newari urban life rested on a sophisticated division of labor supported by fertile land and trade. That social complexity does not make status equal: occupations, religious roles, and access to learning differed. Nor should Valley categories be stretched over Jumla, Doti, Lumbini, or other communities whose languages and institutions had distinct histories.

Painted manuscripts, wooden book covers, and devotional cloth paintings required prepared surfaces, pigments, brushes, precise hands, and practiced composition. Museum collections preserve the finished achievement more readily than the spilled pigment or sore fingers. The joke is gentle; Newar artists' skilled work for Buddhist and Hindu patrons was real.

sections.title: Medicine, health, healing, and evidence limits

items.text: The Durbar Library catalog lists medicine among Nepal's preserved manuscript genres beside religion, astronomy, poetry, drama, and politics. That cataloged range makes learned medical texts visible, but not their use in 1492. A library list cannot prove that a village practitioner owned, read, or followed any particular work.

An institutional manuscript record describes Sanskrit material on Ayurvedic diagnosis and treatment written in Nepalakshara script on birch bark. Its date is not secure. The object therefore demonstrates textual transmission, not a hospital register, and cannot reveal how often families saw healers, treated injuries, or paid for care.

Neither the exact civilization index nor the polygon records illness, childbirth, injury, disability, epidemics, sanitation enforcement, bedside care, or oral remedies. Those repository files establish scope and geometry only. The card refuses to convert a mapped label into health statistics, named clinics, or equal access across western communities.

An undated Nepalakshara manuscript on birch bark preserves Sanskrit material on Ayurvedic diagnosis and treatment. Because its date is not secure, it cannot be assigned to this eight-year window. It is included to show a manuscript tradition and the discipline required to say “we do not know” when chronology will not cooperate.

Wellcome's “Ayurvedic Man” comes from eighteenth-century Kathmandu, roughly three centuries later. It shows how medical bodies could be diagrammed in a later manuscript, but it is not a picture of 1490s practice. No reviewed source supports exact rates of illness, named clinics, vaccination, or one uniform healing system across the polygon.

sections.title: Water, waste, toilets, achievements, and the seam

items.text: Kathmandu Valley water systems linked royal canals, ponds, tanks, recharge areas, and sunken stone spouts. Archaeology and inscriptions trace important elements earlier than this card. The network supported cultivation and domestic collection in the excluded Valley, but the evidence does not map every channel working in 1492 or every household carrying water.

A peer-reviewed review explains that hiti systems captured, conveyed, filtered, and publicly delivered water. That is a major engineering achievement, not automatic proof of modern plumbing. Water had to be collected, carried, stored, and kept usable, and access could vary by neighborhood, season, maintenance, and social arrangements.

UNESCO notes that public hiti fountains originated in the sixth century and remained communal water sources over generations. Its modern restoration case demonstrates living continuity, not an unchanged medieval routine. A public spout could be technically clever and socially important without piping drinking water into every fifteenth-century kitchen.

The reviewed water sources document channels, ponds, tanks, and public spouts, but no secure 1492 household toilet, sewer network, waste collector, or bathing schedule. A beautifully carved spout is not evidence of a flush toilet; archaeology refuses that upgrade, however convenient it would be.

At 1500 the exact id ends. Tested Nuwakot, Pokhara, and Jumla switch to the atlas's Tibet layer; Doti and Lumbini switch to Delhi Sultanate. People, farms, courts, shrines, manuscripts, and routes continued. The ending is continuity with technical successor labels, not conquest, extinction, or a modern national boundary appearing.

ending.text: The exact “nepal-1492” feature disappears at the 1500 atlas seam. Nuwakot, Pokhara, and Jumla are relabeled “tibet,” while Doti and Lumbini are relabeled “delhi-sultanate.” Neither broad label proves uniform conquest or ownership. Valley Malla courts, western principalities, pilgrimage places, households, and trade routes continued beyond the software handoff.
